subsystems.name: Physical qubit lattice
subsystems.role: a checkerboard of data qubits and measure qubits that together encode one logical qubit.

subsystems.name: Qubit hardware platform
parts: superconducting transmon circuits on silicon, or neutral atoms in optical tweezers

subsystems.name: Stabiliser measurement cycle
subsystems.role: repeatedly interrogates the lattice to detect bit-flip and phase-flip errors without collapsing the encoded state.

subsystems.name: Classical decoder
subsystems.role: turns the syndrome history into the most likely error chain and a correction.

subsystems.name: Feedback and logical operations
subsystems.role: applies corrections and performs gates on the encoded qubit.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the qubit chip
buildSteps.detail: Josephson junctions, resonators and couplers are patterned on a silicon wafer using lithography; neutral-atom versions instead load atoms into an optical tweezer array.

buildSteps.title: Lay out the lattice
buildSteps.detail: Data and measure qubits are arranged in a 2D grid with couplers only between neighbours, so each stabiliser touches its four surrounding data qubits.

buildSteps.title: Cool, tune and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Superconducting chips are cooled to about 10 millikelvin; qubit frequencies, gate amplitudes and readout are calibrated one by one.

buildSteps.title: Benchmark physical errors
buildSteps.detail: Randomised benchmarking and tomography measure single-qubit and two-qubit error rates; these must sit below the code's threshold.

buildSteps.title: Run repeated stabiliser cycles
buildSteps.detail: A fixed sequence of gates and measurements extracts syndromes round after round, building a spacetime history of detection events.

buildSteps.title: Decode in real time
buildSteps.detail: A matching or neural decoder processes each syndrome batch before the next arrives, inferring where and when errors occurred.

buildSteps.title: Apply corrections and compare distances
buildSteps.detail: Logical error rate is measured for distance 3, then 5, then 7; success means it falls roughly by a constant factor each step — below-threshold behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Add logical gates
buildSteps.detail: Lattice surgery merges and splits encoded patches; non-Clifford gates require magic states distilled from many noisy copies.

prerequisites.why: the surface code and its threshold theorem, developed from the late 1990s, prove that sufficiently low physical error rates allow arbitrarily reliable logical qubits.
two-qubit gate fidelities above roughly 99% and fast, accurate readout are needed to sit under threshold; leading platforms now reach this in small systems.
decoding must finish within a few microseconds; fast decoders are demonstrated but scaling to large lattices is unresolved.
each physical qubit needs control and readout lines, and thousands of them must be multiplexed without adding heat or noise.
universal computation needs non-Clifford gates, supplied by distilling many noisy magic states into a few clean ones at high overhead.

pathway.milestone: small surface-code lattices operating below threshold
pathway.unlocks: logical error rates that shrink as the lattice grows — the core proof that scaling the hardware can beat scaling the errors. Google reported this on its Willow processor in 2024 for distances 3, 5 and 7.

pathway.milestone: larger lattices with real-time decoding and encoded Clifford gates
pathway.unlocks: logical qubits that stay correct for long enough to run multi-step circuits.

pathway.milestone: magic-state distillation and fault-tolerant non-Clifford gates
pathway.unlocks: universal fault-tolerant computation, the point at which algorithms like Shor's can run at scale.

pathway.milestone: many logical qubits with practical error rates
pathway.unlocks: quantum computers able to outperform classical machines on chemistry, materials and cryptanalysis problems.
